services.name: Fire sprinkler contractors
services.what: They design, install, inspect, test and repair water-based fire suppression systems: sprinklers, standpipes, fire pumps, backflow preventers and fire department connections. Many firms split installation from inspection, testing and maintenance (ITM). Some also retrofit homes with residential sprinklers.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: the building code decides whether a building needs sprinklers, based on occupancy, area, height and construction (in practice most new mid-size and larger commercial, institutional and multi-unit residential buildings). Once a system is installed, the owner must keep it inspected, tested and maintained for as long as the building is occupied. Homes: sprinklers are optional for most single-family homes in Canada. The US model IRC has required them in new one- and two-family homes since 2009, but most states have removed or blocked that requirement (California and Maryland are notable exceptions). Some municipalities require them for large or remote homes.

standards.CA: Installation: NFPA 13 (commercial), NFPA 13R (low-rise residential) and NFPA 13D (one- and two-family dwellings), referenced by the NBC and provincial building codes. Inspection, testing and maintenance: NFPA 25, referenced by the NFC and provincial fire codes. Standpipes: NFPA 14. Fire pumps: NFPA 20.
standards.US: Installation: NFPA 13, 13R and 13D, referenced by the IBC/IRC and NFPA 101. ITM: NFPA 25, adopted through the IFC/NFPA 1 or state fire code. NFPA 25 does not cover NFPA 13D home systems, which are maintained under the installer's and manufacturer's instructions. Standpipes: NFPA 14. Fire pumps: NFPA 20.

services.frequency: Under NFPA 25 (same in Canada and the US, since both reference it; local amendments vary): control valves inspected weekly if sealed, or monthly if locked or electronically supervised. Gauges: quarterly on wet systems, more often on dry systems. Waterflow and tamper alarm devices tested quarterly or semi-annually depending on type. Annual full inspection, main drain test, and trip test for dry/preaction systems. Fire pumps run weekly or monthly (no-flow churn) plus an annual flow test. 5-year internal pipe and check-valve assessment and standpipe/FDC hydrostatic work. Sprinkler heads sampled or replaced at 50 years (20 years for fast-response, 10 years for dry pendent). The quarterly, semi-annual and annual tasks are usually bundled into one service contract.

credentials.CA: Installers: a licensed sprinkler trade (Ontario's Sprinkler and Fire Protection Installer 427A is a compulsory trade; Red Seal 'Sprinkler System Installer' elsewhere; in Quebec, a CCQ 'mécanicien en protection-incendie' card and an RBQ contractor licence). BC: inspectors must be ASTTBC Registered Fire Protection Technicians with the 'WA' (water-based) designation, and Vancouver rejects tags without it. Membership in CASA (Canadian Automatic Sprinkler Association) is a good sign but not a licence. Design on larger buildings is sealed by a professional engineer (P.Eng).
credentials.US: A state or local fire-protection contractor licence (e.g., California CSLB C-16 'Fire Protection Contractor'; Texas State Fire Marshal's Office sprinkler licences; many states license through the state fire marshal). NICET certification in Water-Based Systems Layout (designers) or Inspection & Testing of Water-Based Systems (ITM techs), with Level II or higher common for lead technicians. NFSA or AFSA membership. Plan sets sealed by a PE where the AHJ requires.

services.cost: Annual ITM contract (bundling the quarterly, semi-annual and annual tasks): about US$200–500 (CA$275–700) for a small building under 10,000 sq ft and about 50 heads; US$500–1,500 (CA$700–2,100) for 10,000–50,000 sq ft; US$1,500–3,000+ for larger buildings. 5-year internal inspection and FDC work is billed extra, about US$1,000–5,000+ (fireprotectionfinder.com 2026 guide). Residential sprinklers: about US$0.80–2 per sq ft in new construction and US$2–7 per sq ft as a retrofit in an existing home (Bob Vila cost guide, Dec 2023; treat as a floor for 2025–2026). Retrofits run higher where a new water service or tank and pump is needed.
vet: Ask for the licence number for your province or state (and the ASTTBC 'WA' designation in BC, or NICET Inspection & Testing of Water-Based Systems in the US), then check it in the regulator's online lookup.
Ask whether their annual report follows the NFPA 25 forms, and whether it lists deficiencies separately from recommendations. A report that says 'all good' with no tested items listed is a red flag.
For a home retrofit, ask whether they will run a hydraulic calculation on your actual water supply (flow test or meter size) before quoting.
Ask who seals the design drawings and who files the permit with your building department.
Red flag: pressuring you to replace all heads at once without showing the NFPA 25 age or condition trigger (50/20/10-year rules, corrosion, paint, recalls).
Ask whether they also service fire pumps and backflow preventers, or whether you will need a second vendor.

services.name: Fire alarm contractors
services.what: They design, install, verify, inspect and repair fire alarm systems: control panels, smoke and heat detectors, pull stations, horns and strobes, and the wiring that connects them. In Canada a new or altered system needs a formal verification before occupancy, then an annual inspection with a written report. They also replace interconnected smoke and CO alarms in multi-unit residential buildings.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: the building code decides whether a fire alarm system is required, based on occupancy and occupant load (e.g., most assembly, care, multi-unit residential, and larger business, mercantile and industrial buildings). Once it is installed, the owner must have it tested annually. Homes: single-family homes need code-required smoke alarms (and CO alarms where there is a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage), but not a fire alarm 'system' or a contractor. Landlords of multi-unit buildings usually do.

standards.CA: Installation: CAN/ULC-S524. Verification of new or altered systems: CAN/ULC-S537. Annual inspection and testing: CAN/ULC-S536, referenced by the NFC and provincial fire codes. Ontario moved to CAN/ULC-S536-19 for annual inspections from 1 Jan 2026, with every device tested individually (no sampling) and longer reports. Smoke alarms: CAN/ULC-S531. Integrated systems testing: CAN/ULC-S1001 (adopted in Quebec's code and others).
standards.US: NFPA 72 (National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code) covers installation, ITM and household alarms. It is adopted through the IBC/IFC or NFPA 1/NFPA 101, with NFPA 70 (NEC) for wiring. Integrated systems testing: NFPA 4. The state or local edition adopted can lag the current NFPA edition.

services.frequency: Canada: annual inspection and test of the whole system by a qualified technician (CAN/ULC-S536), plus owner checks set out in the fire code (daily trouble-light check, and monthly checks of batteries and a rotating manual station in many provinces). US (NFPA 72, Ch. 14): most initiating and notification devices tested annually, batteries and some equipment semi-annually, and smoke detector sensitivity checked within a year of installation and then every 2 years. Both: household smoke alarms replaced at 10 years; CO alarms replaced per the manufacturer (typically 7–10 years).

credentials.CA: Ontario: the Fire Code requires people who do annual tests or repairs to have completed a program acceptable to the Fire Marshal. In practice that means CFAA Registered Technician (or an equivalent ECAO/electrician-based program). BC: ASTTBC Registered Fire Protection Technician with the 'AL' designation. Elsewhere: CFAA registration is the de facto national credential. Installation work also needs a licensed electrical contractor (e.g., ESA/ECRA licence in Ontario; RBQ licence and CMEQ membership for electrical contractors in Quebec).
credentials.US: A state or local fire-alarm or low-voltage contractor licence (e.g., California CSLB C-10 Electrical, or C-7 Low Voltage depending on scope; Texas SFMO fire alarm licence). NICET certification in Fire Alarm Systems or Inspection & Testing of Fire Alarm Systems, with Level II commonly asked for. Factory-authorized dealer status for the panel brand (so they can get parts and software).

services.cost: Annual inspection and testing for a small commercial building: about US$200–1,000+ (CA$275–1,400+) (Safe and Sound Security 2026 guide). Ontario contractors say S536-19 inspections take 20–35% longer than before, so expect Ontario quotes to rise by about that much. New commercial system: about US$1–3 per sq ft in new construction and US$4–12 per sq ft as a retrofit in an occupied building, or US$2,000–10,000 under 5,000 sq ft. Labour about US$100–200 per hour.
vet: Ask for the technician's CFAA registration number (Canada), ASTTBC 'AL' (BC) or NICET level (US), not just the company's credentials. The person on site is the one who must be qualified.
Ask whether their annual report is on the current CAN/ULC-S536 (or NFPA 72) forms and lists every device tested. Sampling is no longer acceptable in Ontario.
Ask whether the panel is proprietary, so only one dealer can program it. If so, get the service rates in writing before you sign.
Ask how they handle deficiencies: a written list with prices, which you then sign off on.
Red flag: an 'inspection' finished in an hour on a multi-floor building, or no inspection tags or report left on site.

services.name: Fire alarm monitoring stations
services.what: Monitoring companies run 24/7 receiving centres that take alarm, supervisory and trouble signals from a building's fire alarm panel and call the fire department and the owner. The contract is often sold by the alarm or security dealer and carried out by a listed central station (sometimes a separate wholesale company). They also run the communicators (cellular, IP or phone-line) that send the signals.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: required where the building code, fire code or insurer calls for off-site monitoring. This is common for sprinklered buildings (monitoring sprinkler waterflow), many assembly, care and multi-unit residential occupancies, and higher-hazard buildings. Ontario requires S561-compliant monitoring for most commercial buildings that need one. Homes: optional. Monitored smoke and heat detectors are usually added to a home security plan and may earn an insurance discount.

standards.CA: CAN/ULC-S561 (installation and services for fire signal receiving centres and systems), referenced by the NBC/NFC and provincial codes. The receiving centre should be listed by ULC. Local monitoring rules may add more requirements.
standards.US: NFPA 72 Chapter 26 (supervising station alarm systems: central, proprietary and remote station). Central stations are commonly UL-listed to UL 827 (or FM Approved). A 'UL Certificate' for the alarm service may be required by the AHJ or insurer.

services.frequency: Continuous monitoring. Signal communication paths are tested on the schedule set by S561 or NFPA 72 (automatic periodic test signals, at least every 24 hours in NFPA 72), and the monitoring connection is checked during the annual fire alarm inspection. Review the call list with the provider at least once a year.

credentials.CA: Ask for the ULC listing of the monitoring station that actually receives your signals (not only the dealer's), plus the ULC certificate of monitoring if your building needs one. The installing dealer should hold the alarm credentials listed under 'alarms'. Security-industry membership (CANASA) is a plus.
credentials.US: A UL 827 listed central station (check the UL Product iQ directory) or an FM Approved one. Ask whether they can issue a UL Certificate if your AHJ or insurer requires it. Some states license alarm companies (e.g., California BSIS Alarm Company Operator; Texas). ESA membership is a plus.

services.cost: Commercial fire alarm monitoring: about US$30–100 per month (CA$40–140), depending on points and communicator type (Safe and Sound Security 2026; Mammoth Security, Aug 2026). UL certificate, where required: about US$495–1,295 per year. Home monitored smoke and heat detection is usually a small add-on to a security plan. Cellular communicators that replace copper phone lines cost extra up front.
vet: Ask: which monitoring station receives my signals, and what is its ULC (S561) or UL 827 listing number?
Ask what happens on a trouble or supervisory signal, not just a fire alarm. Who gets called, and how fast?
Ask how signals are sent (dual-path cellular/IP vs. one phone line) and who pays when the carrier retires the old network.
Ask for the contract length, the auto-renewal terms and the cancellation fee. Multi-year auto-renewing contracts are a common trap.
Red flag: a dealer that cannot name its central station or show its listing.

services.name: Fire extinguisher service companies
services.what: They supply, inspect, maintain, recharge and pressure-test portable fire extinguishers, and tag each unit with the service date. Most also handle Class K (kitchen) extinguishers, extinguisher cabinets and signage, and often staff training. Many also service emergency lighting and kitchen systems on the same visit.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: almost every commercial, industrial, institutional and multi-unit residential building must have portable extinguishers, sized and placed under NFPA 10 as referenced by the fire code, and keep them serviced. Commercial kitchens also need a Class K unit. Homes: extinguishers are recommended but not required. Rechargeable home units can be serviced by these firms; disposable ones are simply replaced.

standards.CA: Selection, installation, inspection and maintenance: NFPA 10, referenced by the NFC and provincial fire codes. Extinguisher ratings and construction are certified to CAN/ULC-S508 and related ULC standards. S508 covers how extinguishers are rated, not how they are serviced.
standards.US: NFPA 10, adopted through the IFC/NFPA 1 and NFPA 101. Ratings: UL 711 and the related UL product standards. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.157 adds workplace requirements, including employee training where staff are expected to use extinguishers.

services.frequency: Both countries (NFPA 10): monthly visual check, done by the owner or staff and recorded on the tag or electronically. Annual maintenance by a qualified technician. 6-year internal maintenance for stored-pressure dry-chemical units. Hydrostatic test every 12 years for dry chemical and every 5 years for water, CO2, wet chemical (Class K) and foam units. Recharge after any use.

credentials.CA: BC: ASTTBC Registered Fire Protection Technician with the 'EX' designation. Other provinces: certification by the provincial fire marshal or a recognised training program is common (e.g., college extinguisher technician courses, CFAA in some regions). Ask what your province's fire code requires. Membership in the Canadian Fire Safety Association is a plus.
credentials.US: Many states license extinguisher companies and technicians through the state fire marshal (e.g., California State Fire Marshal portable extinguisher licence; Texas SFMO extinguisher licence). Look for NAFED membership and the NAFED/ICC Certified Portable Fire Extinguisher Technician credential. Requirements vary a lot between states.

services.cost: Annual maintenance: about US$15–22 per extinguisher (CA$20–30), plus a trip charge or minimum. 6-year maintenance about US$40–60 per unit. 12-year hydrostatic test about US$75–110 per unit. Recharge about US$25–55 depending on agent and size (Serviced Fire Equipment, Florida 2026 pricing; other regions run higher). Many firms quote a per-unit rate plus a base trip fee.
vet: Ask for the technician's licence or certification number (ASTTBC 'EX' in BC, the state fire marshal licence in the US) and make sure it appears on the tag.
Ask for an itemized per-unit price before they arrive. Red flag: 'you need all new extinguishers' without showing the date, damage or hydro-test due date that requires it.
Ask whether their minimum or trip fee is waived when they also service your kitchen system or emergency lights on the same visit.
Ask whether they will check placement and travel distance against NFPA 10, not just tag what is already on the wall.
Ask whether 6-year and hydro-test work is done in-house or sent out, and how long you will be without the units (do they leave loaners?).

services.name: Commercial kitchen fire suppression and hood cleaning contractors
services.what: Suppression contractors install and service the pre-engineered wet-chemical systems in a commercial cooking hood. These systems detect fire over the appliances, release agent and shut off the fuel. A separate trade, exhaust (hood) cleaners, removes grease from hoods, filters, ducts and fans. The two jobs are often sold together but are different skills and credentials.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: any commercial kitchen with grease-producing cooking under a hood (fryers, griddles, charbroilers, woks, ranges) must have a listed hood suppression system and a Class K extinguisher. NFPA 96 sets this in the US; in Canada, NFPA 96 is referenced by the NBC/NFC and provincial codes. That includes restaurants, cafeterias, food trucks in many jurisdictions, churches and community halls with commercial lines. Homes: not applicable.

standards.CA: Ventilation and fire protection: NFPA 96, referenced by the NBC/NFC and provincial codes. Wet-chemical systems: NFPA 17A. System units are tested to ULC/ORD-C1254.6, the Canadian counterpart to UL 300. Class K extinguishers: NFPA 10. Some cities add hood-cleaning rules (e.g., Vancouver requires ASTTBC 'CO' technicians).
standards.US: NFPA 96, adopted through the IFC/NFPA 1. Wet-chemical systems: NFPA 17A. Systems listed to UL 300. Class K extinguishers: NFPA 10. Hood cleaning: NFPA 96 Ch. 11–12 and ANSI/IKECA C10 (cleaning) and I10 (inspection) are widely used.

services.frequency: Suppression system: inspected and serviced every 6 months by a qualified technician (NFPA 96/17A), fusible links replaced on the schedule set by NFPA 17A and the manufacturer, and a 12-year hydrostatic test on agent cylinders. Exhaust system inspected and cleaned by cooking volume (NFPA 96 Table 11.4): monthly for solid fuel (wood or charcoal), quarterly for high volume (24-hour, charbroiling, woks), semi-annually for moderate volume, and annually for low volume (churches, day camps, seasonal). Staff clean filters and check equipment daily or weekly. Class K extinguisher: monthly check and annual service (NFPA 10).

credentials.CA: BC: ASTTBC 'SP' (special suppression) for the system and 'CO' for kitchen exhaust cleaning. Elsewhere: manufacturer factory certification for the system brand (e.g., Ansul, Amerex, Kidde, Pyro-Chem, Buckeye). Ask to see the current certificate, since it expires. Ask your fire department whether there is local hood-cleaner registration.
credentials.US: State fire marshal licensing for pre-engineered kitchen systems in many states (e.g., Texas SFMO; California State Fire Marshal). Current manufacturer certification for the system brand. NICET Special Hazards for some techs. For hood cleaners: IKECA certification (CECS/CESI) or a state or local registration where required.

services.cost: Semi-annual suppression system inspection: about US$150–500 per visit (CA$200–700), depending on hood length, number of tanks and travel (fireprotectionfinder.com). Hood exhaust cleaning is priced separately by hood length, duct run and access. Get two quotes. Fusible links, nozzle caps and recharges after a discharge cost extra.
vet: Ask for the technician's current factory certificate for your system's brand. Uncertified techs may not be able to buy parts or legally service it.
Ask whether your system is UL 300 / ULC-C1254.6 compliant. Older dry-chemical hood systems no longer meet code and must be replaced.
Ask the hood cleaner for before-and-after photos of the duct and fan, not just the hood, and a certificate or label posted at the hood.
Ask whether the suppression contractor will re-check nozzle aiming after any appliance is moved or swapped. A new fryer under old nozzles is a common failure.
Red flag: the cleaner offers to 'skip the ducts' to save money, or leaves no service label.

services.name: Special hazard suppression contractors
services.what: They design and service engineered suppression systems for spaces where water is a poor fit or not enough on its own: server and telecom rooms, electrical rooms, archives, paint booths, industrial processes, flammable liquid storage, and battery energy storage. The systems use clean agents (FM-200/HFC-227ea, Novec 1230/FK-5-1-12, inert gases), CO2, dry chemical, foam or water mist, usually with detection and release panels and room-integrity testing.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: required where the building code, an insurer (often FM Global) or a process standard calls for it, for example spray booths, some flammable-liquid and dip-tank operations, and certain energy storage systems. Owners also often choose them to protect critical equipment or data. Homes: not applicable.

standards.CA: These NFPA standards are referenced by the NBC/NFC and provincial codes for the hazards they cover: NFPA 2001 (clean agent), NFPA 12 (CO2), NFPA 17 (dry chemical), NFPA 11 (foam), NFPA 750 (water mist). Spray booths: NFPA 33. Energy storage: NFPA 855 (adoption varies). Release panels are ULC-listed, and alarm interfaces follow CAN/ULC-S524 and S536. Exactly which standard and edition each province adopts varies, so confirm with the AHJ.
standards.US: NFPA 2001, 12, 17, 11 and 750, adopted through the IFC/NFPA 1. Detection and release under NFPA 72. Spray booths: NFPA 33. Energy storage: NFPA 855. Insurers often add FM Global data sheets (e.g., DS 5-32 for data centres).

services.frequency: Clean agent (NFPA 2001): inspect and test at least annually, check container weight and pressure semi-annually, and run an enclosure-integrity (door fan) check annually or after room changes. CO2 (NFPA 12): semi-annual inspection and agent check, plus periodic hydrostatic testing of cylinders and hoses. Dry chemical (NFPA 17): semi-annual. Detection and release panels: annually with the fire alarm (S536 / NFPA 72). The rules are broadly the same in Canada and the US, since both use the NFPA standards.

credentials.CA: BC: ASTTBC 'SP' designation. All provinces: current manufacturer certification for the system brand (Kidde, Fike, Ansul, Siemens, etc.) and a P.Eng for engineered designs. The detection and release side needs alarm-qualified technicians (CFAA).
credentials.US: NICET Special Hazards Systems (Level II+ for lead techs or designers). State fire-protection contractor licence (e.g., California C-16; Texas SFMO). Current manufacturer certification. FSSA (Fire Suppression Systems Association) membership is a good sign. A PE for engineered designs where the AHJ requires.

services.cost: Too site-specific for reliable public ranges. No trustworthy 2025–2026 cost survey was found. Budget as a service contract (semi-annual visits plus an annual room-integrity test) and get quotes from at least two firms certified on your system's brand. Recharging a clean-agent system after a discharge can cost far more than routine service, so ask about it up front.
vet: Ask whether they are factory-certified on your installed brand, and whether they can buy agent for it. Some agents are going out of production or face phase-down rules, so ask about the supply outlook for yours.
Ask whether the annual visit includes a room-integrity (door fan) test. Without it, the agent may not hold long enough to put out a fire.
Ask how they prevent accidental discharge during testing (abort and lockout procedures). Recharges are expensive.
Ask whether the system's detection and release panel is tied into your building fire alarm and monitoring, and who tests that link.
Red flag: recommending a system type without asking what is being protected and what your insurer requires.

services.name: Fire protection engineers and code consultants
services.what: Licensed engineers who design fire protection and life-safety systems, carry out code reviews and alternative-solution or performance-based designs, and prepare fire safety plans and fire risk assessments. They also act as the owner's representative during construction and handover. They are hired when a contractor's design-build is not enough: changes of use, additions, heritage buildings, warehouses with high-piled storage, or disputes with the fire department.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: needed when the building department requires sealed fire protection drawings (most new or altered sprinkler, standpipe and alarm systems in larger buildings), when you change the occupancy or use of a space, add high-piled storage, propose an alternative solution (Canada) or alternative method (US), or need a code-compliance report for a lease, sale or insurer. Homes: rarely, except for complex custom homes, secondary suites in some provinces, or wildfire-zone design reviews.

standards.CA: NBC/NFC and the provincial building and fire codes. Engineering practice is regulated by the provincial or territorial engineering regulators: PEO (Ontario), OIQ (Quebec), Engineers and Geoscientists BC, APEGA (Alberta), etc. In Ontario, designers who are not engineers need a BCIN (Building Code Identification Number) in the relevant category for some small-building work.
standards.US: IBC/IFC or NFPA 1/101 as adopted locally, plus the NFPA system standards. Engineering is licensed by the state engineering boards. The NCEES PE Fire Protection exam leads to a PE licence, and some states license 'fire protection' as a separate discipline.

services.frequency: Project-based, with no fixed cycle. Some jurisdictions require periodic engineering reviews or fire safety plan updates (e.g., Canadian fire codes require fire safety plans to be reviewed at set intervals, commonly at least every 12 months, or when the building changes).

credentials.CA: P.Eng (or ing. in Quebec) in good standing with the provincial regulator. Check the regulator's public register. Ask for proof that fire protection is within their practice area. SFPE membership is a plus. Ontario: a BCIN with fire-protection qualifications for designers who are not engineers.
credentials.US: A PE licence in your state (check the state board's lookup), ideally earned through the PE Fire Protection exam. SFPE membership, and NFPA's CFPS (Certified Fire Protection Specialist) for non-engineer consultants.

services.cost: No reliable public rate survey was found. Firms usually quote a fixed fee per task (code review, drawing package, alternative solution). Small-building code reviews often fall in the low thousands of dollars, and full system design scales with building size. Treat these as rough planning numbers only and get two proposals.
vet: Ask for their licence number and check it on the provincial or state register. Fire protection must be within their declared scope.
Ask for two or three similar projects in your jurisdiction, and whether they have dealt with your local fire department before.
Ask whether they will stamp the drawings and handle the permit back-and-forth, or only advise.
Ask whether they are independent of the installing contractor. A design-build contractor's engineer works for the contractor, not for you.
Red flag: promising approval of an alternative solution before reviewing the building.

services.name: Fire safety training and fire safety plan providers
services.what: They train staff to use extinguishers (often with live-fire or digital simulators), run fire drills, train fire wardens and supervisory staff, and write or update the building's fire safety plan and evacuation diagrams. Many extinguisher and alarm service companies offer this as an add-on. Independent consultants and some fire departments also provide it.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: Canadian fire codes (NFC Section 2.8 as adopted provincially) require a fire safety plan, trained supervisory staff and regular fire drills for many occupancies, including assembly, care, multi-unit residential and high buildings, and others where a fire alarm is installed. In the US, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38 requires an emergency action plan for many employers, and 1910.157(g) requires annual extinguisher training where employees are expected to use extinguishers. NFPA 101 and the IFC set drill rules by occupancy. Homes: optional. Families can use free fire department programs and home escape planning.

standards.CA: NFC Section 2.8 (emergency planning, fire safety plans, fire drills) as adopted provincially, e.g., Ontario Fire Code Section 2.8 and Quebec Code de sécurité. Workplace health and safety rules in each province add employer duties. Provinces vary, so confirm drill frequency with your fire department.
standards.US: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38 (emergency action plans), 1910.39 (fire prevention plans) and 1910.157(g) (extinguisher training). NFPA 101 / IFC Ch. 4 for drills and plans by occupancy. NFPA 10 for extinguisher use.

services.frequency: Canada: fire drills at intervals set by the fire code for your occupancy (commonly at least annually, and more often for care, school and some high-rise occupancies). Supervisory staff trained and the fire safety plan reviewed at least every 12 months or when the building changes. US: extinguisher training at hire and annually (OSHA 1910.157), with drills per NFPA 101 / IFC by occupancy (e.g., schools monthly during the school year; many businesses annually).

credentials.CA: There is no single licence. Look for trainers with fire service, CFAA or CFSA backgrounds, or recognised certifications such as NFPA CFPS. In some provinces the fire department must approve the fire safety plan, so ask whether the provider's plans are usually approved first time.
credentials.US: There is no single licence. Look for NFPA CFPS, former fire-service instructors (NFPA 1041 Fire Instructor), or OSHA-authorized outreach trainers. Training must cover the specific extinguishers and hazards on site.

services.cost: No reliable public price survey was found. Providers typically charge per session (on-site group class) or per person, and add a fee to write or update a fire safety plan. Extinguisher companies often discount training when it is bundled with annual service. Get quotes that list exactly what is delivered: plan, diagrams, warden training, drill observation and a written report.
vet: Ask whether the training is hands-on (live fire or a simulator) or classroom-only. OSHA requires 'familiarization' with the general principles of extinguisher use; hands-on practice is better.
Ask whether they will write the fire safety plan to your province's fire code (or your OSHA emergency action plan) and submit it to the fire department if approval is needed.
Ask for attendance records and certificates you can keep for inspectors and insurers.
Ask whether they cover your actual hazards (kitchens, lithium batteries, flammable storage), not a generic deck.
Red flag: online-only 'certification' sold as meeting OSHA's hands-on expectations or fire code supervisory staff rules.

services.name: Chimney sweeps and wood-heat inspectors
services.what: Chimney sweeps clean creosote and soot from chimneys and flue pipes, inspect liners, caps and masonry, and repair or reline chimneys. In Canada, WETT-certified technicians also install and inspect wood stoves, fireplaces and pellet appliances to the installation code, often for insurers and home sales. Gas fireplaces and vents are a separate licensed gas trade.
services.whoNeeds: Homes: anyone burning wood, pellets or oil, or with a chimney serving a furnace or boiler. Canadian insurers often require a WETT inspection before they will cover a wood stove or fireplace, and you must disclose wood and pellet stoves to your insurer or risk a denied claim. Businesses: restaurants with wood-fired ovens (also covered under NFPA 96 solid-fuel rules), cottages and rentals, and any building with solid-fuel heating.

standards.CA: Installation: CSA B365 (solid-fuel appliances), CSA B139 (oil), and CSA B149.1 (gas, via provincial gas regulators such as TSSA in Ontario). Chimney inspection and cleaning are required by the NFC and provincial fire codes, which require chimneys and flue pipes to be inspected regularly and cleaned as needed. Some provinces reference NFPA 211. The exact interval wording varies by province.
standards.US: NFPA 211 (chimneys, fireplaces, vents and solid-fuel appliances), adopted through the IFC/IRC or state code. Inspection levels 1, 2 and 3 are defined in NFPA 211. NFPA 54 (gas) and NFPA 31 (oil) for those appliances.

services.frequency: US: NFPA 211 calls for annual inspection of chimneys, fireplaces and vents, plus cleaning as needed. A Level 2 inspection is required on a property sale, when the appliance or fuel changes, or after a chimney fire or seismic event. Canada: an annual inspection is the widely followed rule (fire codes require regular inspection and cleaning as needed). Heavy wood users may need cleaning more than once a season. A WETT inspection is typically done on purchase, before insurance coverage, or after installation.

credentials.CA: WETT certification (WETT Inc.), e.g., SITE Inspector or SITE Comprehensive Inspector, or Chimney Sweep and Installer designations. Verify it in the WETT directory. Quebec: APC (Association des professionnels du chauffage) certification is common, and installers need an RBQ licence. Gas fireplaces: a provincially licensed gas technician (e.g., TSSA-registered contractor with a G2/G3 technician in Ontario).
credentials.US: CSIA Certified Chimney Sweep (CCS), verified on CSIA's Find a Pro. NCSG (National Chimney Sweep Guild) membership. NFI (National Fireplace Institute) certification for hearth installers. A state contractor licence for masonry or relining where your state requires it.

services.cost: US: chimney cleaning averages about US$400 (typical US$100–500). Level 1 inspection plus sweep runs US$85–950 and Level 2 US$150–1,000, varying by appliance (gas fireplace US$85–250, pellet US$175–350, wood stove US$200–500, wood fireplace US$300–1,000). Level 3 is US$500–5,000 (Fixr, Jan 2025). HomeGnome puts a typical sweep at US$110–350. Canada: WETT says there is no national price list and price depends on distance, level and number of appliances. Planning range about CA$150–450 for a sweep or a WETT visual inspection (converted from the US ranges, not surveyed).
vet: Ask for their WETT number (Canada) or CSIA CCS number (US) and look it up in the directory.
Ask which inspection level they will perform (WETT Visual/Technical/Invasive, or NFPA 211 Level 1/2/3) and what written report you get. Insurers usually want a WETT report form.
Ask whether they will camera-scan the flue on a home purchase or after a chimney fire.
Red flag: a 'free' or very cheap sweep that turns into an urgent relining sale with no photos. Ask for camera footage before agreeing to major repairs.
Gas appliances: ask whether the person holds a provincial or state gas licence. A chimney sweep certification alone does not cover gas work.

services.name: Wildfire mitigation and home-hardening specialists
services.what: They assess homes and properties in the wildland-urban interface and reduce the risk of ignition from embers and flames. Typical work: clearing the 0–1.5 m (0–5 ft) noncombustible zone, thinning vegetation, ember-resistant vents, gutter guards, Class A roofing, and removing combustibles near the house. Assessors write the plan, and landscaping, roofing and construction trades do the work. Exterior sprinkler and foam systems are a niche add-on.
services.whoNeeds: Homes: anyone in or near forest, grassland or interface areas, especially in BC, Alberta, the Northwest Territories and wildfire-prone parts of other provinces, and in the western US. Insurers in high-risk areas increasingly ask for mitigation, and California, Colorado and others have defensible-space or wildland-urban-interface building codes. Businesses: rural and resort properties, campgrounds, cottages and rentals, and properties where insurers or municipalities require a FireSmart or defensible-space plan.

standards.CA: FireSmart Canada guidance (Home Ignition Zone: 0–1.5 m noncombustible zone, then 1.5–10 m, 10–30 m and 30–100 m zones). The National Guide for Wildland-Urban Interface Fires (NRC, 2021) is guidance, not code, unless a municipality adopts it. Some BC and Alberta municipalities set wildfire development permit areas.
standards.US: NFPA 1140 (Wildland Fire Protection, which absorbed NFPA 1144) and the ICC International Wildland-Urban Interface Code (IWUIC) where adopted. California: Chapter 7A of the California Building Code and PRC 4291 defensible space. The IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home designation (voluntary, in 14 states) is used by some insurers.

services.frequency: Reassess once a year before fire season and after major landscaping or building changes. Clear gutters, roofs and the noncombustible zone several times a season. FireSmart and IBHS designations have renewal or recertification cycles; check the current terms.

credentials.CA: FireSmart-trained assessors: Local FireSmart Representatives, and FireSmart BC Home Partners Program Wildfire Mitigation Specialists, who do free assessments. FireSmart BC says homeowners should never be charged for a FireSmart assessment. Contractors doing tree or structural work should have the right trade credentials (ISA-certified arborist, roofing licence, WorkSafe coverage).
credentials.US: NFPA Certified Wildfire Mitigation Specialist (CWMS). State or county defensible-space inspectors. IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home third-party evaluators. Licensed tree and roofing contractors for the physical work.

services.cost: Canada: FireSmart home assessments are free through FireSmart BC's Home Partners Program and many municipalities, and nobody should charge for a FireSmart assessment. US: IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home has a US$125 non-refundable application fee, with the owner doing the work and a third party evaluating it. Mitigation work (vent replacement, gutter guards, noncombustible zone, tree work) ranges from a few hundred dollars of DIY to tens of thousands for a roof replacement. Get line-item quotes from each trade.
vet: Ask whether the assessment follows FireSmart Canada's Home Ignition Zone (or NFPA 1140 / IBHS) and whether you get a written, prioritized plan.
In Canada, red flag: anyone charging for a 'FireSmart assessment'. The official program is free.
Ask whether the specialist has the NFPA CWMS credential (US) or FireSmart training (Canada), and whether they are independent of the contractor selling the work.
Ask your insurer which designation, if any, it recognises before paying for one.
Red flag: pitching exterior sprinkler or foam systems before the zero-to-1.5 m zone, vents and gutters are fixed. Embers ignite most homes.

services.name: Emergency lighting and exit sign service
services.what: They install, test and repair battery-pack emergency lights, remote heads, exit signs (including the green 'running man' signs now required in new Canadian buildings), and the inverters or generators that power them. Annual work usually means a full-duration battery discharge test and replacing failed batteries and lamps. Fire extinguisher and alarm companies often do this on the same visit.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: most commercial, institutional, industrial and multi-unit residential buildings need emergency lighting along exit routes and lit exit signs under the building code. Owners must test and maintain them under the fire code. Homes: not required in single-family homes.

standards.CA: NBC Section 3.2.7 (emergency lighting) and 3.4.5 (exit signs, pictogram style in NBC 2010 and later). Maintenance under NFC Section 6.5 and provincial equivalents (e.g., Ontario Fire Code Section 6.5). Unit equipment is certified to CSA C22.2 No. 141. Emergency generators: CSA C282.
standards.US: NFPA 101 Sections 7.9 (emergency lighting) and 7.10 (exit marking), or IBC/IFC Section 1008/1013 where adopted. Generator-backed systems: NFPA 110/111. Electrical: NFPA 70 (NEC) Article 700. Equipment listed to UL 924.

services.frequency: US (NFPA 101): monthly functional test of at least 30 seconds and annual 90-minute full-duration test on battery units. Self-testing units still need a monthly visual check of the indicator. Generators tested monthly under NFPA 110. Canada (NFC 6.5 as adopted): monthly inspection or test of unit equipment, and an annual test for the rated duration, which is usually set by the building code (often 30 minutes for many occupancies, longer for some high or care buildings). Check your province's fire code for exact wording.

credentials.CA: BC: ASTTBC 'EM' designation (emergency power and lighting) and 'GS' for generators. Other provinces: a licensed electrical contractor for wiring and repairs (ESA/ECRA in Ontario; CMEQ/RBQ in Quebec). Testing is often done by fire-protection technicians.
credentials.US: A licensed electrical contractor for installation and repair (state or local licence). Testing can be done by a trained person, but many AHJs expect a fire-protection service company's report. NFPA 110 generator testing should be done by the generator service provider.

services.cost: No reliable public price survey was found. It is usually billed per fixture on a service visit (often bundled with extinguisher service), with batteries and lamps extra. Ask for per-fixture test and per-battery replacement prices in writing.
vet: Ask whether the annual test is a full-duration discharge (90 minutes under NFPA 101; the code-set duration in Canada) or just a push-button check. Only the full test meets the annual requirement.
Ask for a fixture-by-fixture report with battery dates.
Ask whether they hold the right designation or licence (ASTTBC 'EM' in BC; an electrical licence for repairs).
Ask whether they will flag non-pictogram exit signs or dark spots on exit routes, without forcing replacements the code does not require for your building.
Red flag: replacing every battery pack on every visit regardless of test results.

services.name: Firestopping and passive fire protection contractors
services.what: They seal openings where pipes, cables and ducts pass through fire-rated walls and floors, install fire-rated joint systems, and repair or inspect fire separations and fire doors. This keeps fire and smoke contained to the compartment where they start. The work must match a tested, listed system for each kind of opening, so it is a specialist trade rather than 'caulking'.
services.whoNeeds: Businesses: any building with code-required fire separations, such as multi-unit residential, offices, hospitals, schools, hotels and mixed-use buildings. It is needed during construction and after any renovation, cabling or plumbing work that cuts through a rated assembly. Fire doors in rated walls also need inspecting. Homes: in single-family homes only the attached-garage separation, and for duplexes, townhouses and condos the suite separations.

standards.CA: NBC Subsection 3.1.9 (penetrations) and 3.1.8 (fire separations and closures). Firestop systems are tested to CAN/ULC-S115. Fire separations must be maintained under the NFC Section 2.2. Fire doors are installed and maintained to NFPA 80, referenced by the NBC/NFC.
standards.US: IBC Chapter 7 (Sections 714–715) and the IFC/NFPA 101 maintenance rules. Firestop systems tested to ASTM E814 / UL 1479, and joints to UL 2079 / ASTM E1966. Field inspection to ASTM E2174 (penetrations) and E2393 (joints). Fire doors: NFPA 80, including an annual inspection, and NFPA 105 for smoke doors.

services.frequency: No fixed cycle for firestopping. Inspect when building and after any trade work through rated assemblies, and include it in periodic fire code inspections. Fire doors: inspected and tested annually under NFPA 80 in the US, and checked under the NFC's closure-maintenance rules in Canada.

credentials.CA: Look for FM 4991 Approved or UL Qualified Firestop Contractor status (both available in Canada), FCIA membership, and the contractor's ability to name the exact ULC or cUL listed system used at each penetration. Fire doors: DHI-certified inspectors.
credentials.US: FM 4991 Approved Firestop Contractor or UL Qualified Firestop Contractor, plus an FCIA member with a firestop 'DIIM' (Designated Individual) on staff. Special inspection agencies accredited to IAS AC291 for third-party inspection. DHI Fire Door Assembly Inspector (FDAI) for annual NFPA 80 door inspections.

services.cost: No reliable public price survey was found. Work is usually priced per penetration or per linear foot or metre of joint, plus mobilization. Fire door annual inspections are usually priced per door. Ask for a penetration count and the listed system numbers in the quote.
vet: Ask: are you FM 4991 Approved or UL Qualified Firestop? Then check the FCIA directory.
Ask for the tested system number (ULC/cUL/UL) for each type of penetration in your quote and close-out package.
Ask whether they label each firestopped penetration and provide a photo log.
Ask who is responsible when another trade (cable or plumbing) later breaches the seal, and whether they offer a re-inspection.
Red flag: 'we just use fire caulk', with no listed system for the specific wall, pipe material and size.

programs.name: Wildfire Mitigation Program — free certified home assessment

programs.name: FireSmart BC Coordinators
programs.note: Local coordinators run neighbourhood assessments and community FireSmart activity in most regional districts.

programs.name: TNRD FireSmart Homeowner Rebate
programs.note: Thompson-Nicola Regional District reimburses homeowners for qualifying wildfire-resistant upgrades. Check your own regional district too — several run comparable programs.

programs.name: City of Kamloops FireSmart assessments and rebates

programs.name: FireSmart Alberta
programs.note: Provincial coordination of community assessments, the Neighbourhood Recognition Program and local vegetation-management support.

programs.name: RMWB FireSmart Rebate Program
programs.note: The Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo reimburses residents for wildfire-resistant home upgrades.

programs.name: FireSmart Saskatchewan (SPSA)

programs.name: Saskatchewan First Nations Emergency Management — FireSmart
